nodes.title: Off-policy evaluation is defined by a ratio whose denominator is the logging propensity — absent it, the estimator is undefined, not noisy
nodes.body: Off-policy evaluation estimates V(pi_e) from data produced by pi_b, and the whole importance-sampling family (IPS, WIS, PDIS, PDWIS, DR) is built on the ratio rho = prod_t pi_e(a_t|x_t) / pi_b(a_t|x_t). Voloshin, Le, Jiang & Yue (arXiv:1911.06854, COBS benchmark, thousands of experiments) test three folk beliefs — DR beats direct and IS; horizon is the primary driver of OPE failure; model-based is the go-to direct method — and report the truth is "much more nuanced". The reusable part is the precondition, not the ranking: IPS "often assumes known pi_b", and estimating pi_b from data yields "a potentially biased estimator". When the logging policy never assigned the action, the denominator is zero rather than small, so the estimator is undefined. Applies to dsh-loom: loopPolicy chooses candidates, minGain, stopping and lesson exposure, and 0 of 458 attempt.finished records carry the probability with which any policy was in force. Test in our ledger: grep every event type for a policy snapshot — round.started carries only {n, taskId, chainVersion} across all 230 occurrences, so this is a logging gap before it is a statistical one.
nodes.source: arXiv:1911.06854 (Voloshin, Le, Jiang, Yue), COBS benchmark, github.com/clvoloshin/OPE-tools

nodes.title: Our replay is an exact re-decision of recorded numbers: zero variance, zero external validity
nodes.body: src/loop/replay.js re-decides recorded rounds: bestOf(attempts, budget) slices the logged attempt pool by candidate budget, requires verifierOk !== false, computes delta = score - incumbent.score and promotes when delta >= minGain - 1e-9. Its own header states the scope honestly: replay "cannot re-run agents, so a policy that would have sampled different tasks or prompted differently is *not* simulated". That makes it a deterministic, zero-variance estimator of exactly one quantity — the promotion count induced by a threshold on a fixed score pool. It cannot be a confidence-bearing estimator because repeating it returns the identical number. Candidate count enters only as truncation (bestOf slices, never draws), knowledge changes the prompt and is invisible to replay, halving and the stopping rule are not modelled at all. Applies to dsh-loom: comparePolicies' verdict "candidate-better" is a statement about counterfactual gate arithmetic, not about the loop. Test in our ledger: run comparePolicies twice on one campaign with the same arguments — the verdict is bit-identical, so no interval exists by construction.
nodes.source: src/loop/replay.js header comment and replayRounds/comparePolicies implementation in this repo

nodes.title: A switchback converts carryover into a bias term linear in the switch rate: |tau_SB(lambda) - tau_TOT| <= 4 M lambda (1 + t0)
nodes.body: When the unit of randomisation is time rather than a user, a switchback alternates treatment and control on the same unit and the previous interval's carryover is the bias. The Stanford causal-inference notes (Theorem 15.4) give |tau_SB(lambda) - tau_TOT| <= 4 M lambda (1 + t0) for |Y_t| <= M under Markovian switchback with switch rate lambda, with consistency whenever lambda_T -> 0 and T lambda_T -> infinity: fast switching shrinks bias and starves variance. Bojinov, Simchi-Levi & Zhao (Management Science 69(7):3759-3777, 2023) derive the optimal switch rate under alternate assumptions on the order of carryover and give a subroutine that identifies that order from two i.i.d. units, e.g. two well-separated time spans on one unit. Applies to dsh-loom: rounds within a campaign are one unit in time and carryover is mechanical — a promoted patch changes the tree the next round starts from — so the switch rate is a knob to declare, not to discover. Test in our ledger: campaigns have median 2 rounds and only 6 of 70 reach 8, so lambda_T can never be small and pooling across campaigns is the only route.
nodes.source: causal inference notes (web.stanford.edu/~swager/causal_inf_book.pdf) Thm 15.4; Bojinov, Simchi-Levi, Zhao, Management Science 69(7):3759-3777 (2023), doi 10.1287/mnsc.2022.4583

nodes.title: ITS extrapolates the pre-trend with no untreated group, and breaks when the policy is tweaked soon after the intervention
nodes.body: Interrupted time series extrapolates the pre-intervention trend and attributes the deviation to the intervention; because there is no untreated group, "comparisons are only as good as the model used for extrapolation" (Springer Prevention Science 10.1007/s11121-022-01427-8, Table 3). van Leeuwen, Lugtig & Feskens (PLOS ONE 19(8):e0301301, 2024) run 384 Monte Carlo scenarios x 1,000 datasets: a step change of 30% of the pre-intervention slope needs about 500 subjects with 8 time points (15% needs ~1,100 with 12), a slope change of 0.1 needs 20 time points, and underfitting is a larger obstacle than overfitting — a policy "introduced and then tweaked not long after the initial intervention" biases both step and slope unless an extra segment is modelled with at least two points in each. Applies to dsh-loom: changing loopPolicy mid-campaign is precisely the tweak-after-intervention case, and the fix costs one extra segment per change. Test in our ledger: no campaign has ever run two chain versions, so the design has never been attempted, let alone powered.
nodes.source: van Leeuwen, Lugtig, Feskens, PLOS ONE 19(8):e0301301 (2024), doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0301301; Prevention Science 10.1007/s11121-022-01427-8 Table 3

nodes.title: Non-stationary bandits price the regime change explicitly: a discount window or a changepoint reset, never a pooled average
nodes.body: Non-stationary bandit work replaces the fixed-policy assumption with a moving target. Discounted Thompson Sampling (Qi, Wang & Zhu, arXiv:2305.10718) uses a Gaussian prior with discount gamma and gets near-optimal regret for both abrupt and smooth changes; the discount implies an effective window of roughly gamma^(-1/(1-gamma)) observations beyond which data no longer inform the current policy. Multiscale piecewise-stationary linear bandits (arXiv:2002.05289) instead detect changepoints, run LinUCB inside homogeneous intervals and reset the index at a detected change, and notes that changepoint detection "hasn't been successful due to the extreme difficulty of detecting faint changes". Applies to dsh-loom: our reward is not stationary — round-1 pass rate is 62% (84/135) and falls to 25% by round 8 — so pooling all 458 attempts measures an average over regimes that no longer exist. Test in our ledger: regress round-level pass rate on round number; the monotone decline is already visible in the raw scores and needs no new instrumentation.
nodes.source: arXiv:2305.10718 (Qi, Wang, Zhu, Discounted Thompson Sampling); arXiv:2002.05289 (Multiscale Non-stationary Stochastic Bandits)

nodes.title: With unknown propensities the target is a set, not a point: report a sensitivity-bounded interval
nodes.body: When the logging propensity is unknown or confounded the policy value is not point-identified and the honest output is an interval. Kallus & Zhou (Confounding-Robust Policy Evaluation / Improvement) optimise worst-case value over a sensitivity model bounding the deviation between nominal and true propensities; Bennett & Kallus (NeurIPS 2019, Policy Evaluation with Latent Confounders via Optimal Balance) prove that with proxies for latent confounders "there exist no single set of weights that give unbiased evaluation regardless of outcome model, unlike the case with no unobserved confounders where density ratios are sufficient"; arXiv:2301.08649 delivers finite-sample coverage for the out-of-sample loss under "model misspecification, including unmeasured confounding" via marginal sensitivity. Applies to dsh-loom: any policy comparison should emit an interval plus the sensitivity parameter, instead of the current single verdict string. Test in our ledger: gate.evaluated already emits checks{...} on 211 decisions, so widening the output is cheap; what is missing is the sensitivity parameter, which needs at least one deliberate policy variation to calibrate.
nodes.source: Kallus & Zhou, Confounding-Robust Policy Evaluation; Bennett & Kallus, NeurIPS 2019; arXiv:2301.08649 Off-Policy Evaluation with Out-of-Sample Guarantees

nodes.title: Voloshin et al. 2019/2020: the OPE benchmark whose most useful output is the precondition, not the ranking
nodes.body: Voloshin, Le, Jiang & Yue, "Empirical Study of Off-Policy Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning", arXiv:1911.06854 (v1 2019-11-15, v2 2020-02-25; code at github.com/clvoloshin/OPE-tools, COBS benchmark). Thousands of experiments spanning the IPS family (IS, PDIS, WIS, PDWIS), direct methods (model-based/AM, FQE, Retrace, Q-Reg, MRDR, IH) and hybrids (DR, MAGIC), explicitly designed to test three commonly held beliefs — that doubly robust beats direct and IS, that horizon length is the primary driver of OPE failure, and that model-based is the go-to direct method — with the conclusion that the reality is "much more nuanced". For our purposes the durable content is the assumption list rather than the leaderboard: every IS-family estimator divides by pi_b(a_t|x_t) and the paper concedes IPS "often assumes known pi_b", while estimating it from data gives a "potentially biased estimator". Applies to dsh-loom: cite this whenever someone proposes "just do off-policy evaluation on the ledger" — the denominator does not exist in our records.
nodes.source: arXiv:1911.06854v2, https://arxiv.org/html/1911.06854v2 (fetched 2026-11-12)

nodes.title: Bojinov, Simchi-Levi & Zhao 2023: switchbacks exist because unit-level randomisation leaks, and carryover order is identifiable
nodes.body: Bojinov, Simchi-Levi & Zhao, "Design and Analysis of Switchback Experiments", Management Science 69(7):3759-3777 (2023), doi 10.1287/mnsc.2022.4583 (working paper WP21-034, hbs.edu). The motivating problem is interference: randomising at the driver level leaks because a treated driver changes what control drivers see, so the city is aggregated into a single unit and treatment is randomised in time. The paper derives the optimal switchback design under alternative assumptions about the order of the carryover effect and supplies a subroutine that identifies that order using two i.i.d. units (e.g. two well-separated time spans) by comparing optimal designs under two candidate orders. Applies to dsh-loom: campaigns share a workspace and a lesson store, so our units interfere by construction and the switchback framing is the right one; the carryover-order question maps onto "how many rounds does a promoted patch keep affecting scores", which is what our lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.742 is measuring.
nodes.source: Bojinov, Simchi-Levi, Zhao, Management Science 69(7):3759-3777 (2023), doi 10.1287/mnsc.2022.4583, WP21-034

nodes.title: dsh-loom logs outcomes richly and its own decision policy almost not at all
nodes.body: A dsh-loom round is plan -> attempts -> verifier gate -> promote-if-better, governed by loopPolicy fields minGain, candidates, knowledge, halving, holdoutSlack, planMode (src/loop/policy.js; defaults minGain 0.05, candidates null, knowledge true, halving true, holdoutSlack 0.02, planMode full). What the ledger records about that policy is close to nothing: 230 round.started events carry only {n, taskId, chainVersion}; 211 gate.evaluated events carry {candidateId, round, promoted, score, incumbentScore, checks}; there are exactly 4 campaign.policy events across 70 campaigns and all four set models or planMode, none touching minGain or candidates. The policy in force at any decision is therefore reconstructible only by guessing defaults from source, and a change leaves no fingerprint to align with outcomes. Applies to dsh-loom: stamping the effective policy (or its hash) on round.started and gate.evaluated is the single highest-value instrumentation change, and validatePolicyOverride/diffPolicy already compute everything needed. Test in our ledger: after stamping, count distinct policy hashes per campaign; today the count of observable policy changes is 4 and zero are gate-related.
nodes.source: src/loop/policy.js; src/runtime/round.js:1985; ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns events.jsonl (this repo's own ledger, read 2026-11-12)

nodes.title: The gain axis is degenerate: 191 of 211 gate decisions are first decisions, 16 are ties, exactly 1 is a real delta
nodes.body: Of 211 gate.evaluated decisions, 191 (90.5%) have incumbentScore null, i.e. the gate had no prior score for that task and promotion was decided without any comparison; 16 have delta 0 and all 16 were rejected; exactly 1 has delta 1 and was promoted. Score is binary, so the delta axis has two values and the one that matters has n=1. Under the shipped replay (minGain 0.05, candidates 2) over 230 recorded rounds the delta histogram is {0: 78, 1: 61} and contains nothing else. Applies to dsh-loom: any threshold tuned on this data is tuned on a 1-bit contrast, and minGain cannot be identified from our logs because the smallest non-zero delta is 1.0 — every threshold in (0, 1] sits strictly inside the same gap. Test in our ledger: replay at minGain 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.999 and 1 all return 61 promotions; this is measurable today and was measured.
nodes.source: own computation over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/events.jsonl: 211 gate.evaluated records, 230 replay decisions

nodes.title: Nine declared minGain settings produce exactly two outcomes; the only live breakpoint is whether ties promote
nodes.body: Running the shipped replayRounds over all 69 campaigns at minGain in {0, 0.001, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.999, 1} yields exactly 2 distinct results: 139 promotions at minGain 0, of which 78 are ties with delta 0, versus 61 promotions at every setting in (0, 1]. The knob is declared on [0, 1] and behaves as a boolean whose only breakpoint is tie handling. Since the real gate rejects ties (delta >= minGain - EPSILON with minGain 0.05 rejects delta 0, and the ledger shows 16 such rejections), the last 78 promotions are an artefact of the replay default rather than a policy choice. Applies to dsh-loom: rsi_replay's headline question — "would a stricter gain bar have promoted less and ended lower?" — has the answer "no, not once above 0" on our data, and the entire content of the difference is the tie rule. Test in our ledger: this is a direct execution of src/loop/replay.js against C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns; a denser grid confirms the step is at 0 and nowhere else.
nodes.source: own computation: node probe over src/loop/replay.js and ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns (69 campaigns, 230 rounds)

nodes.title: Candidate count is the only policy field with a measurable effect: 2 -> 1 flips exactly 9 of 69 campaigns
nodes.body: Replaying with minGain 0.05 and candidates 1 gives 52 promotions and a final-score sum of 52 across 69 campaigns; candidates 2 gives 61 and 61. Per campaign, comparePolicies(2 -> 1) returns candidate-worse in 9 of 69 campaigns and no-difference in 60, with zero candidate-better. The ledger itself ran 2 candidates in 225 of 227 rounds, so the 1-candidate arm is entirely counterfactual and the 9 campaigns are the only evidence that candidate count matters at all. Because the mechanism is truncation (bestOf slices the recorded list), the effect is exactly reproducible and needs no statistics — but it also says nothing about whether a second candidate would have produced a different patch, since replay never generates one. Applies to dsh-loom: this is the one knob where replay has real content, and its content is "if you had stopped reading after the first attempt, 9 campaigns would have ended on a lower final score". Test in our ledger: rerun _compare_probe.mjs; the 9 flips are stable and their task ids are the natural unit for a clustered check.
nodes.source: own computation: comparePolicies per campaign over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns (69 campaigns)

nodes.title: Task id explains 59.2% of score variance: ICC 0.485, design effect 2.66, effective n ~172 not 458
nodes.body: Across 458 scored attempts on 101 distinct tasks the between-task sum of squares is 59.2% of total; the one-way ICC is 0.485 with an average cluster size of 4.43, giving a design effect of 1 + (4.43 - 1) x 0.485 = 2.66 and an effective sample size of about 458/2.66 = 172 (SE inflated by 1.63x). Pass rates on tasks with n >= 6 range from 0% to 100% with median 33%: card-actions 2/48, head-dot 4/40, queue-wait 2/28, node-attribution 1/18 versus plateau 11/12, deferred 11/12, sampling 7/8, exposure 8/10. Applies to dsh-loom: any policy comparison that does not block on task is mostly a comparison of which tasks each arm happened to draw, and with 70 campaigns drawing from 104 eval task ids that confound is live. Test in our ledger: cluster-bootstrap by task id on the 9 candidate-count flips; if they concentrate in three tasks the "9 of 69" is closer to n=3.
nodes.source: own computation: one-way ANOVA ICC over 458 attempt.finished scores joined to round.started taskId

nodes.title: Within-campaign round scores have lag-1 autocorrelation 0.742 and P(repeat) 0.874 — rounds are not independent trials
nodes.body: Over the 10 campaigns with at least 4 scored rounds (97 observations, 87 adjacent pairs) the lag-1 autocorrelation of round-level score is 0.742 and P(same outcome as the previous round) is 0.874. The effective independent sample is therefore far below the nominal count, and any pre/post or switchback analysis that assumes independent rounds understates the standard error by roughly sqrt((1 + r)/(1 - r)) = 2.6 at r = 0.742. Applies to dsh-loom: the carryover is mechanical rather than stochastic — a promotion changes the tree the next round starts from — so this is the treatment leaking across periods, i.e. exactly the carryover term switchback theory prices. Test in our ledger: the statistic is computable today from round.finished.score sequences and should be recomputed after any change to the promotion rule, because the rule itself sets the carryover magnitude. Note the estimate rests on 10 series, so treat 0.74 as an order-of-magnitude warning rather than a precise constant.
nodes.source: own computation: lag-1 correlation of round.finished.score within campaigns with >= 4 rounds

nodes.title: Single-campaign interrupted time series is structurally impossible: only 6 of 70 campaigns reach 8 rounds, median is 2
nodes.body: Rounds per campaign in the ledger: 1 round x 15 campaigns, 2 x 28, 3 x 14, 4 x 2, 6 x 2, 7 x 2, 9 x 1, then a tail with a maximum of 18; only 6 of 70 campaigns reach 8 rounds and the median is 2. The ITS rule-of-thumb minimums are six points (Fretheim), eight (Penfold) or twelve (Wagner), and van Leeuwen et al. 2024 need 8-12 time points plus n around 500-1,100 for a 30%-of-slope step change; they also warn that underfitting biases the estimate when a policy is tweaked shortly after the intervention. Applies to dsh-loom: a policy change introduced at round 3 of a 4-round campaign leaves one post-intervention point, so single-series ITS is not a power problem but an identification impossibility. Test in our ledger: count campaigns with at least two scored rounds on each side of a policy change — currently zero, because no campaign has run two chain versions.
nodes.source: own computation over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns (rounds per campaign) + PLOS ONE 19(8):e0301301 power thresholds

nodes.title: 42.8% of round time (8.8 h of 20.4 h) is spent after the campaign already scored a 1
nodes.body: Of the 160 rounds that carry a duration, 67 ran after the campaign had already scored a 1: 8.8 h out of 20.4 h total round time (42.8%), covering 133 attempts and $0.041 of the $0.111 total spend. A stop-on-first-promotion rule would have skipped 108 of 211 rounds; first promotions by round are round 1 -> 56 campaigns, round 2 -> 3, round 3 -> 1, round 4 -> 1, never -> 6. Against the saving, those same later rounds are the only place the gate can compare a candidate to an incumbent, so they contain 100% of the 17 non-first gate decisions we own. Applies to dsh-loom: the stopping-rule question is not whether stopping saves time (it plainly does, at 42.8%) but whether stopping destroys the only comparative signal we have, and the second half is unmeasured. Test in our ledger: replay the stop-on-first-promotion rule and report final score unchanged for 67 campaigns while non-first gate decisions fall from 17 to 0 — the trade is visible, its value is not.
nodes.source: own computation: round.finished durationMs/costUsd/attemptCount plus first score-1 round per campaign

nodes.title: The one quasi-randomised contrast in the ledger: ITT effect 0.5 pp (p=0.93) versus as-treated 46 pp (p=4e-9)
nodes.body: The only randomised-looking variation the loop ever produced is the phase flag: exposeIndexes() marks exactly one candidate per round as exploit (dosed with lessons) and the others explore. Intention-to-treat by phase is 110/228 = 48.2% versus 112/230 = 48.7%, Fisher p = 0.93, risk difference CI [-9.6, +8.7] pp — no effect. As-treated is 38/42 = 90.5% dosed versus 184/416 = 44.2% undosed, Fisher p = 4.3e-9 — a 46 pp "effect". The gap between the two is compliance: 186 of 228 exploit-arm attempts (81.6%) received no lessons at all, because lessons are gated on policy.knowledge, config.knowledge.enabled and selectLessons returning a non-empty list. Applies to dsh-loom: the exposure experiment already exists in code and would answer a real question, but it is being analysed as-treated and therefore reports a composition artefact. Test in our ledger: instrument the exploit flag rather than the lesson count as the treatment; the 81.6% non-compliance is the number that invalidates the naive estimate.
nodes.source: own computation: attempt.finished phase x lessons x score, 458 attempts; Fisher exact tests

nodes.title: Round 1 decides the campaign: 56 of 67 scored campaigns promote there, and 6 never promote at all
nodes.body: Round 1 carries 63 of 211 gate decisions and 51 of 114 promotions. First-promotion round by campaign: round 1 -> 56, round 2 -> 3, round 3 -> 1, round 4 -> 1, never -> 6 (some campaigns have no scored round). Combined with the 90.5% first-decision share, the loop behaves as a one-shot filter with a long, mostly uninformative tail: 108 of 211 rounds would never have run under stop-on-first-promotion, and the pass rate declines from 62% (84/135) at round 1 to 25% at round 8. Applies to dsh-loom: any between-campaign policy comparison is dominated by the round-1 pass rate, so a design must either hold the round-1 task fixed, block on it, or accept that it is measuring first-attempt quality rather than loop quality. Test in our ledger: stratify the 9 candidate-count flips by whether the flip happened in round 1; if all 9 are round-1 events, candidate count is a round-1 phenomenon and says nothing about later behaviour.
nodes.source: own computation: gate.evaluated promoted-by-round and round.started linkage over 70 campaigns

nodes.title: Our own 94%-versus-33% lesson effect collapses to 5-vs-4 under era, slot and treatment-definition corrections
nodes.body: The tempting reading is 47/50 = 94% pass with notesShown=1 versus 57/175 = 33% without, Fisher p = 5.7e-13, odds ratio about 32. Three corrections kill it. (i) Era: all 50 notesShown=1 a2 attempts sit in the 136 modern-era attempts (failureKind null, pass rate 84.6%) while most of the 57 without sit in the 322 older attempts (33.2%); within the modern era the contrast is 47/50 versus 68/74, Fisher p = 0.74. (ii) Slot: exposure is a2 in 50 of 50 cases, and a2's baseline rate differs from a1's. (iii) Treatment definition: notesShown counts board notes, not lessons; the lessons array is non-empty in only 42 of 458 attempts, and on the 42 rounds with exactly one lesson-dosed candidate the paired outcome is 5 treated-only-wins versus 4 control-only-wins, exact sign-test p = 1.0. Applies to dsh-loom: this is our own worked example of an OPE-style estimate manufactured by a confound, and it is why the answer to the topic is a design rather than an estimator. Test in our ledger: the era split is reproducible by filtering on failureKind; publish both numbers or neither.
nodes.source: own computation: notesShown/lessons/phase/failureKind cross-tabs and Fisher tests over 458 attempts

nodes.title: What replay can attribute: gate arithmetic only — and pooling campaigns breaks even that
nodes.body: Decompose replay's content. It can attribute the part of the promotion count that is a deterministic function of (recorded score sequence, minGain, candidate budget): measured as 139 versus 61 promotions across the minGain grid, and 9 campaigns flipping when candidates goes 2 -> 1. It cannot attribute anything that changes the attempt pool, because bestOf only slices recorded attempts: candidate count enters as truncation, knowledge never enters, halving and the stopping rule are unmodelled. A concrete sensitivity: replay over all 69 campaigns with one global incumbent yields 60 promotions against the ledger's 114, while a per-task incumbent (matching bestPriorScore, which keys on task.id) yields 100 — so the estimator's answer depends on an assumption the real gate makes implicitly. Worse, the shipped comparePolicies on a pooled 69-campaign list returns "no-difference" for every pair, because it treats the pool as one sequence with one incumbent. Applies to dsh-loom: replay is a unit test of gate arithmetic, and calling it policy evaluation overstates it by one category. Test in our ledger: per-campaign comparePolicies gives 69 no-difference for minGain 0.05 -> 0.2, 9 candidate-worse for 2 -> 1, and silently clamps an out-of-range minGain of 1.1 to 1 via normalizePolicy rather than rejecting it.
nodes.source: own computation: replayRounds/comparePolicies executed over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns; src/runtime/round.js bestPriorScore semantics

nodes.title: The design that can attribute a loopPolicy change from our own logs: campaign-level switchback with a permanent control stratum and a clustered permutation test
nodes.body: Concretely: (1) randomise the policy choice at campaign level on a pre-declared schedule — a switchback over calendar time with blocks of at least two campaigns, not rounds, because rounds have lag-1 autocorrelation 0.742 and the campaign is the unit that carries a task; (2) stratify assignment by task family (task explains 59.2% of score variance) and by era (pass rate falls 62% -> 25% across rounds); (3) keep one stratum permanently on the incumbent policy as a drift control, so a level shift in the control is separable from the treatment; (4) analyse with a paired sign/permutation test on campaign-level final score plus a task-clustered bootstrap, never a t-test on attempts (design effect 2.66, effective n ~172); (5) report an interval rather than a verdict, since with 51 discordant pairs the detectable shift is ~8.8 pp and 77 pairs are needed for 15 pp; (6) stamp the effective policy hash on round.started, which makes the propensity of the policy assignment itself observable — the precondition that turns this from curve-fitting into OPE. Expected cost: at 70 campaigns a 50/50 split gives n=104 per arm, where the smallest detectable promotion-rate difference is 18.3 pp, so an 8-10 pp question needs roughly 2-3x current campaign throughput or six months of the present rate.
nodes.source: synthesis of own ledger statistics (n-cluster-icc, n-autocorr, n-its-length) with switchback design theory (Bojinov et al. 2023) and paired-test power calculations

nodes.title: Unbounded peeking turns a nominal 5% test into a 26% false-positive generator, and our model decides when to peek
nodes.body: Evan Miller ("How Not To Run An A/B Test", 2010-04-18) computes that with a 50% conversion rate and a stop-as-soon-as-significant rule, the true false-positive rate at nominal 5% is 26.1% when the test is evaluated after every observation; to obtain a true 5% you must report 2.9% after one peek, 2.2% after two, 1.8% after three, 1.4% after five and 1.0% after ten, and the sample size rule is n = 16 sigma^2 / delta^2. Valid alternatives are group-sequential, always-valid confidence sequences or Bayesian designs; a parallel practitioner reference puts daily peeking on a 4-week experiment at ~28 tests with an implied FPR "30 percent or more". Applies to dsh-loom: rsi_replay and rsi_control action=policy are model-callable at any moment and the model chooses when to look, so the loop has unlimited optional stopping with no alpha accounting — 26% is the right prior for any "policy X is better" conclusion produced that way. Test in our ledger: count rsi_replay calls per campaign between policy changes; that count is not logged today, which is itself the finding.
nodes.source: Evan Miller, How Not To Run An A/B Test, evanmiller.org, 2010-04-18; sequential-testing-patterns.md (rampstackco/claude-skills)

nodes.title: DoorDash measured 62% false positives at the wrong unit of analysis; our ICC puts us in the same regime
nodes.body: DoorDash ("Experiment Rigor for Switchback Experiment Analysis", Carla Sneider and Yixin Tang, 2019-02-20) simulated A/A and A/B over weeks of delivery data and compared delivery-level, unit-level, unit-level with variance reduction, and multilevel models. The delivery-level t-test produced a false-positive rate of 0.62 (62%), because nested observations always have ICC > 0 and the OLS variance formula omits the ICC inflation factor; multilevel modelling gave FPR 0.03 at power 0.93 and cut time-to-significance by about 30%, and covariate variance reduction could not compensate for the sample-size loss. Applies to dsh-loom: our own ICC of 0.485 with average cluster size 4.43 implies a design effect of 2.66, so any per-attempt comparison is in exactly the DoorDash failure regime, and the 5-vs-4 paired exposure result is far too small to survive a clustered analysis. Test in our ledger: rerun every per-attempt contrast with a task-clustered bootstrap; the interval should widen by about 1.6x and no current contrast should remain significant.
nodes.source: DoorDash Engineering, Experiment Rigor for Switchback Experiment Analysis, 2019-02-20

nodes.title: At Fin, faster answers raised satisfaction because users read speed as canned macros — the metric moved opposite to quality
nodes.body: Fin/Intercom (Pedro Tabacof, GrowthBook talk and write-up, 2026) report two failures from thousands of live experiments over about three years, 1-2 dozen concurrent at a time, with a measured win rate of roughly 20-30%. First, increasing latency improved positive feedback, because users interpreted an instant answer as a canned macro; latency was therefore a confounder rather than a nuisance and they had to add a third arm holding latency constant. Second, adding conversation history raised positive feedback and hallucinations together — agents promised refunds they could not give — and the positive feedback was partly caused by the hallucinations; a targeted prompt fix roughly halved the gain while removing the hallucination increase. Applies to dsh-loom: our only positive signal is score in {0,1} from a verifier, and a cheaper or faster candidate can score 1 by doing less, so the same direction-of-causation trap is open. Test in our ledger: durationMs, diff.insertions and score are already recorded on 437 attempts; a candidate that scores 1 with a smaller diff and shorter duration is the signature to look for.
nodes.source: Fin/Intercom, Pedro Tabacof, GrowthBook podcast/blog 2026 (secondary summary of experiments at Fin)

nodes.title: GPT-4o sycophancy shipped on good offline evals plus a positive small A/B, over expert objections, and was rolled back in four days
nodes.body: OpenAI's April 2025 GPT-4o sycophancy update went out on offline evals that looked good and a small A/B test where users liked it, while a few expert testers said the behaviour "felt" wrong; the positive quantitative signal overrode the qualitative one and the retrospective calls it "a wrong decision". The model was rolled back after about four days and the stated lesson is that behaviour problems must be treated as launch blockers, because aggregate metrics do not detect what experts detect. Confidence is medium: the primary post page returns 404 on re-fetch and these details come from secondary summaries (CNET 2025-05-04 and several engineering lesson write-ups), so the mechanism is solid while the exact wording is not verified. Applies to dsh-loom: the loop has no expert channel at all — the gate is mechanical, and the only human input is an occasional checkpoint — so it has the failure mode without the corrective. Test in our ledger: no existing measurement; the cheapest partial fix is to log a human veto on promotions and treat a veto as a labelled negative, which the ledger can then count.
nodes.source: OpenAI sycophancy post-mortem, April 25 2025 (page 404 on re-fetch; details via CNET 2025-05-04 and secondary lesson write-ups)

nodes.title: A prompt variant with a LOWER offline eval score produced BETTER live business results
nodes.body: Fin/Intercom report a concrete rank inversion: a prompt variant that scored lower on their offline evaluation produced better business outcomes in a live A/B. That inversion is the stated reason they run A/B over offline evaluation at all, despite offline sets of only ~1k-10k examples versus millions of live samples within days, at 1-2 dozen concurrent experiments and an estimated 20-30% win rate (which they say is not formally tracked because the denominator is hard). The general mechanism is that the offline distribution and the live distribution diverge, and the offline metric is a proxy whose errors are not symmetric. Applies to dsh-loom: our replay is an offline evaluator of exactly this kind — deterministic, cheap, and currently the only one — so a replay verdict of candidate-better carries no guarantee about live loop output. Test in our ledger: we can construct the inversion ourselves by taking the replay-preferred policy, applying it live for N campaigns, and comparing final scores; today no campaign has ever run two policies, so the test has never been run and the inversion is unmeasured rather than unlikely.
nodes.source: Fin/Intercom, Pedro Tabacof, GrowthBook podcast/blog 2026 (offline-vs-online rank inversion, offline set sizes 1k-10k)

nodes.title: Zero campaigns have ever run two chain versions, and all 4 policy writes are model or planMode tests
nodes.body: In 70 campaigns the number that ran more than one chainVersion is 0, and the only policy writes in the entire ledger are 4 campaign.policy events: one {"planMode":"off"} and three {"models":{...}} failover tests (a deliberately bad worker model, a haiku worker with a flash fallback, a fallback-only run). No event records minGain, candidates, halving, holdoutSlack or knowledge being set, and no campaign ran an A/B on any policy field. Meanwhile the loop changed its code far more often: 96 chain.proposed and 69 chain.activated events. Applies to dsh-loom: "policy improvement" is currently a hypothesis with n=0, not a measured activity, and the loop has optimised its pipeline while never testing the rule that decides what to promote. Test in our ledger: the counts are directly computable — 0 campaigns with two chain versions, 4 policy events, 0 gate-related — and they explain why no attribution design exists today.
nodes.source: own computation: campaign.policy/chain.proposed/chain.activated events and per-campaign chainVersion sets over 70 campaigns

nodes.title: What is the outcome? Today a promotion means the verifier passed on this task, not that the campaign made progress
nodes.body: This question gates every design in this file. The ledger score is gateOk ? 1 : 0 where gateOk = verifier.ok && outcomeKind === 'ok', so a promotion means "this candidate passed a verifier on this task", not "the campaign moved toward its objective". Evidence that the score is not progress: 191 of 211 gate decisions are first decisions, 56 of 67 scored campaigns promote in round 1, and 6 campaigns never promote at all; pass rate then declines from 62% to 25%, which is consistent with an instrument that gets harder rather than with a loop that gets worse. A stopping rule or a gate threshold cannot be evaluated against an outcome that saturates in round 1. Applies to dsh-loom: the missing quantity is a per-campaign objective that survives a promotion — a held-out suite pass rate over time, or the campaign's declared eval-set mean — and holdout data exists for only 58 rounds. Test in our ledger: correlate holdout pass with final score across the 58 rounds carrying a holdoutId; if they disagree, the current score is not the target and no amount of policy testing on it will help.
nodes.source: own computation: score construction in src/runtime/round.js (scoreAttempt, gateOk) plus gate.evaluated/holdout.selected counts

edges.note: The benchmark's durable output is the assumption list: IPS divides by a known pi_b, and estimating pi_b gives a potentially biased estimator.
The precondition is a logged logging policy; dsh-loom logs no such probability, so the precondition fails rather than degrades.
0 of 458 attempts carry the probability of the action taken, so no importance weight can be formed at all.
When the propensity is unknown, the honest output is a sensitivity-bounded interval rather than a point estimate — the usable version of the same idea.
A randomized policy assignment plus an interval report is the practical route to a partially identified comparison without propensities in the logs.
Switchback bias is linear in the switch rate under Markovian carryover, and the carryover order is identifiable from two i.i.d. units per the paper's subroutine.
Our measured lag-1 of 0.742 is an estimate of exactly the carryover the switchback bias term prices.
Mechanical carryover from a promoted patch is why rounds cannot be treated as independent blocks.
ITS needs 6-12 points per segment; our median campaign has 2 and only 6 of 70 reach 8, so the design cannot be instantiated per campaign.
Discounting or changepoint segmentation is the bandit-side answer to the same non-stationarity that breaks naive ITS extrapolation.
Pass rate falls 62% to 25% across rounds, so era must be a blocking factor rather than a nuisance regressor.
The scope comment in replay.js is the same claim the analysis measures: exact on recorded numbers, silent on the attempt pool.
If 191 of 211 decisions lack an incumbent and only one delta is non-zero, a threshold on delta can only have one live breakpoint.
The two-outcome result at nine settings is the replay-side measurement of the same degeneracy the ledger shows.
The minGain grid is the direct evidence that replay's attribution is boolean, not graded.
The 9-of-69 flip is the one place replay has real content, and it is a truncation effect rather than a sampling effect.
A deterministic offline evaluator with zero variance cannot detect the offline-online inversion; that is the inversion's mechanism inside our own tooling.
The 52-versus-61 promotion count and the 9 campaign flips are the measurement that separates gate arithmetic from policy effect.
Our ICC 0.485 and design effect 2.66 put per-attempt analyses squarely in the regime where DoorDash measured 62% false positives.
Task explains 59.2% of score variance, so the outcome is mostly a property of which task was drawn, not of the loop.
Blocking on task family is not a refinement of the design; it is a precondition given a 2.66 design effect.
The 0.5 pp ITT versus 46 pp as-treated gap is the compliance-driven artefact that the collapse analysis explains.
The era, slot and treatment-definition corrections are computed on the same 458 attempts.
It is a worked example of what happens when the treatment probability is not logged: an as-treated estimate 90 times too large.
56 of 67 campaigns promote in round 1, which is why 90.5% of gate decisions have no incumbent to compare against.
A one-shot filter cannot be evaluated by a stopping rule or a threshold; the outcome has to be defined past round 1.
42.8% of round time runs after the first 1 exactly because promotion happens so early in almost every campaign.
Any stopping-rule arm must account for the 8.8 h and 133 attempts of post-promotion work it removes.
Because per-campaign series are too short, the switch must be at campaign level and the analysis pooled.
A pre-declared schedule is the only defence against a model that can call rsi_replay whenever it likes.
If a lower offline score can produce a better live outcome, only a live randomised comparison can settle the question.
A proxy metric can move opposite to quality, which is what our binary verifier score is at risk of doing.
Aggregate metrics missed what experts saw; our loop has no expert channel, so the outcome definition carries all the weight.
Because the policy is not stamped on rounds, policy changes are invisible; the 4 campaign.policy events are the only trace.
The n=0 result is computed from the same event fields that show the logging gap.
The proposed design cannot be retrofitted; it fails on today's ledger because no campaign ever carried two policies.
A randomized comparison is worthless if the endpoint saturates in round 1, so the outcome must be defined first.
The switch rate and block length are the design's free parameters and their bias cost is the theorem's linear term.
As the evaluation instrument only; replay remains the arithmetic unit test that the design should keep running.
The 9-campaign flip looks like evidence at the campaign unit but would be a false-positive generator at the attempt unit — the two readings disagree about what counts as n.
The 42.8% post-promotion spend is only waste under the current outcome definition; under a drift-detection objective it is the whole measurement.

gaps: What is the per-campaign objective that does not saturate in round 1? The ledger scores gateOk (verifier passed on this task), 191 of 211 gate decisions have no incumbent, and 56 of 67 campaigns promote in round 1 — so no existing field measures progress after a promotion.

Has any dsh-loom campaign ever changed its own loopPolicy (minGain, candidates, stopping) rather than its chain? Only 4 campaign.policy events exist and none touch the gate, but the events may predate the policy surface, so the true historical count is unknown.

What is the carryover order of a promotion — one round, several, or until the next task switch? Lag-1 autocorrelation within campaign is 0.742 on 10 series, but the switchback identification subroutine needs two i.i.d. units per order, which our campaigns do not provide.

Does the 55% promotion rate differ between parallel and cascade candidate mode at equal candidate count? candidateMode is logged as parallel in 152 rounds and cascade in none, so the comparison has never existed.

Would a stop-on-first-promotion rule lose anything measurable? It would skip 108 of 211 rounds and 42.8% of round time, but the 17 non-first gate decisions it would delete are the only incumbent comparisons we own, so the value side is unmeasured.

Can rsi_replay calls be counted per campaign between policy changes? Optional stopping is the main threat to any claimed policy effect and the calls are not currently logged, so the peeking rate is unknown.
Do the 9 candidate-count flips concentrate in round 1 and in a few task ids? If they do, the only non-trivial policy effect we can measure is a round-1 artifact with effective n near 3.

Is the binary verifier score a proxy that can invert against real progress, as latency did at Fin? durationMs, diff.insertions and score are all recorded, so the check is computable, but no one has run it.

What would a policy-switch design cost in wall-clock at current throughput? At 70 campaigns a 50/50 split gives n=104 per arm, where the smallest detectable promotion-rate difference is 18.3 pp, so an 8-10 pp question needs 2-3x the campaign rate.

Does the holdout pass rate (58 rounds carry a holdoutId) track the campaign final score? If holdout and final score disagree, the current generation rule is optimising the wrong quantity and every policy verdict inherits the error.
